title: A Harvard Study Found the Best Diet for Weight Management During Menopause. Indian Kitchens Already Follow Most of It.
excerpt: A 38,000-woman study in JAMA Network Open found that a planetary health diet cut obesity risk by 54 per cent during menopause. Dal, whole wheat roti, nuts, and mustard oil — staples of Indian cooking — are at the core of what researchers recommend.
body:
The question of what to eat during menopause has been debated for decades. A new study from Harvard just offered the clearest answer yet — and it looks remarkably like a traditional Indian thali.

Researchers at Brigham and Women's Hospital, led by Dr Tong Xia, analysed data from 38,283 women in the Nurses' Health Study II over a 12-year period surrounding menopause. They compared how closely women adhered to several established dietary patterns and tracked weight gain and obesity risk. The results, published in *JAMA Network Open*, found that two dietary approaches stood out from the rest.

## The Winning Diets

The Planetary Health Diet Index (PHDI) was associated with a 54 per cent reduction in the risk of developing obesity during menopause. The reverse Empirical Dietary Index for Hyperinsulinemia (EDIH), which measures how much a diet avoids spiking insulin, showed a 49 per cent reduction.

Both diets share common principles: high intake of nuts, legumes, whole grains, vegetables, fruits, and unsaturated oils. Low intake of red and processed meats, sodium, and fried foods. The PHDI was specifically designed by the EAT-Lancet Commission to be both healthy for humans and sustainable for the planet.

The average weight gain in the study was 0.80 kg per year across all women. Those adhering most closely to the low-insulinemic diet gained 0.28 kg less per year — a difference that compounds significantly over a decade.

## Why This Matters for South Asian Women

The planetary health diet's core components read like a shopping list from an Indian grocery store. Whole wheat (atta), lentils (dal), chickpeas (chana), nuts (almonds, cashews), mustard oil, sesame oil, spinach, okra, cauliflower — these are not exotic recommendations for Indian families. They are Tuesday dinner.

But the diaspora shift is real. Second-generation Indian Americans and immigrant families who have adopted more processed, Western dietary patterns often move away from these traditional foods precisely when they need them most. Menopause typically hits between ages 45 and 55, a period when many South Asian women in the US are managing careers, ageing parents, and teenagers simultaneously. Convenience foods fill the gap.

The Harvard study suggests that returning to or maintaining traditional Indian cooking patterns — with some adjustments — may offer meaningful protection against the weight gain and metabolic changes that accompany menopause.

## What the Study Does and Does Not Say

The researchers tracked foods with the strongest positive correlations with weight management: nuts, unsaturated oils (like mustard oil, not ghee or butter), whole-grain carbohydrates, and vegetable protein. Foods most associated with weight gain included red and processed meats, sodium-heavy dishes, and fried foods like French fries.

This does not mean all Indian food is automatically healthy. Heavily fried snacks, excessive ghee, and white rice-heavy diets do not align with what the study recommends. The benefit comes from the dal-sabzi-roti-salad framework, not the samosa-paratha-mithai framework.

The study also found that these results were consistent whether women were premenopausal, going through menopause, or postmenopausal. The protective effect was not limited to a narrow window.

## The Practical Takeaway

For South Asian women approaching or going through menopause, the research supports a straightforward approach: prioritise traditional whole foods, increase nut and legume intake, use unsaturated cooking oils, and reduce processed and fried foods. No special supplements needed. No radical dietary overhaul required.

"Incorporating this dietary guidance into routine midlife care may help prevent obesity and support long-term cardiometabolic health in women," the authors wrote.

The foods your mother made were not just comfort food. According to Harvard, they may be the best prescription for the decade ahead.

*Sources: JAMA Network Open (May 2026); Brigham and Women's Hospital, Harvard Medical School; Clinical Advisor; Medscape*
